analysis.one_liner: Makes large farms pay far more of the real cost of federally subsidized irrigation water.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it sat in the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee from July 1990 until Congress ended in January 1991.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal dam and irrigation projects in the West deliver water to farms at prices that cover only part of what construction actually cost taxpayers. This bill would have required irrigation water sold under new federal contracts to repay a substantial share of those construction costs, required sales of subsidized 'excess' farmland to happen at fair market value, banned automatic renewal clauses in federal water contracts, forced unstarted projects to be evaluated using real market prices instead of discounted assumptions, and required farms growing certain surplus crops to pay half, then all, of the full cost of delivering that water. In short, it would have scaled back one of the largest remaining subsidies to big western agriculture.
analysis.who_benefits: Federal taxpayers, who currently cover the gap between what it costs to build and run federal irrigation projects and what water users are charged. Over time, it also could have discouraged growing surplus crops on federally subsidized water and the inflation of land values that come with cheap water rights.

how_it_helps.text: The bill required the price of irrigation water under new federal water service contracts to recover 'an appropriate and substantial share' of the fixed costs of construction, not just operation and maintenance charges.
It required sales of subsidized excess lands to nonexcess owners after enactment to be at fair market value related to irrigation water delivery, with the proceeds deposited in the Treasury.
It repealed the authority for renewal clauses in Bureau of Reclamation water service contracts, ending a mechanism that locked in below-cost water pricing.

It required the Interior Department to evaluate all unstarted reclamation projects using the June 1987 federal procedures based on market commodity prices, which produce more honest cost-benefit numbers than the older discounting approach.

It required farmers using federal water to produce crops under a federal acreage reduction program — crops in surplus — to pay 50 percent of full delivery cost on contracts entered two years after enactment, and at least full cost after four years.

analysis.who_pays: Large western farm operations and irrigation districts that receive heavily subsidized federal water. Their water bills would rise, and land tied to subsidized water would sell at fair market value rather than carrying below-market water rights. Smaller farms in the same districts would face some of the same higher water costs, though the full-cost requirement is aimed at water used for surplus program crops.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large western farms on subsidized water

drawbacks.text: Higher irrigation water costs would not fall only on the largest operations; family-size farms in the same districts would also pay more, and some of the cost could be passed through to food prices at the margin.

The bill contained carve-outs: it did not apply to irrigation on individual Indian or tribal lands with deferred repayment, to contracts whose users were already paying 20 percent of construction costs in cash, or to the Garrison Diversion Unit, softening the reform.

Repealing contract renewal authority and repricing water would have disrupted long-standing water contracts that western communities and lenders rely on, creating transition uncertainty for districts that had planned around existing terms.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core of the bill — making water users repay a substantial share of construction costs, pricing land sales at fair market value, and charging full cost for water used on surplus crops — targets a genuine, long-running transfer from taxpayers to a concentrated group of western water users, and it does so with phase-ins and limited exemptions rather than abruptly. Its main weaknesses are that smaller farms in the same districts share the cost and that the exemptions dilute the reform. On balance the public benefit clearly outweighs the costs, which is what makes its quiet death in committee notable.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in late July 1990, sent to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee and then to its Water and Power Subcommittee, and never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 101st Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator John Heinz introduced the Reclamation Reform and Integrity Act of 1990 on July 30, 1990, with no cosponsors.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources on July 30, 1990.
The next day it was referred to the Subcommittee on Water and Power, where no further action was taken.
No committee markup, hearing, floor vote, or House action appears in the bill's action history before the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The western irrigation districts and large farm operations that would have paid more for federal water are better off; taxpayers continue covering the difference between project costs and what water users are charged.

for.name: Sen. John Heinz
for.role: U.S. Senator from Pennsylvania; sole sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and put forward a package repricing federal irrigation water, requiring fair market value land sales, and charging full cost for water used on surplus crops.

against.name: Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee leadership
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over reclamation law
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to the Water and Power Subcommittee, where it sat with no hearing, markup, or vote before Congress ended.

against.name: Western irrigation districts and large farm water users
against.role: Recipients of below-cost federal reclamation water
against.what_they_did: Long-standing, well-documented opposition to full-cost water pricing and to tightening reclamation subsidy rules, which shaped how politically difficult such bills are to move.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the only recorded supporter was a single Republican senator with no cosponsors, so no party split can be measured.

industries.industry: Western irrigated agriculture (irrigation districts and large farm water users)
industries.note: The bill would have forced these operations to pay a substantial share of construction costs and eventually full cost for water used on surplus program crops, ending a subsidy the public has funded. Their cheap-water advantage is paid for by taxpayers.

industries.industry: Landowners and buyers of subsidized 'excess' reclamation lands
industries.note: Sales of excess lands to nonexcess owners would have had to be at fair market value tied to water delivery, ending sales that embed subsidized water value in land prices.

industries.industry: Water project construction and engineering interests
industries.note: Requiring market-price evaluation of unstarted projects would likely have killed some marginal projects, reducing future construction work, while projects that passed the honest test would still be built.
